extracted.intended_audience: university technology transfer officers, research administrators, and university contract negotiators
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on federal rights, markings, and licensing for DOD/DOE/NASA/other-agency technical data and computer software delivered under contracts, grants, and cooperative agreements; aimed at advising universities how to protect IP and negotiate appropriate rights. Covers categories of rights, marking/justification requirements, agency-specific deviations, and grant-era data-sharing policies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Government purpose rights (DOD)
rubrics_metrics.description: Government purpose rights give the government broad rights in DOD technical data (not limited to DOD) and may extend to use in government contracts; they are more limited than unlimited rights but allow a wide range of government and contractor activities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typical DOD government-purpose rights duration is five years beginning at the start of the contract (which may be short relative to commercialization timelines). During that initial five-year period the contractor has exclusive commercial rights; administrators should consider negotiating a longer government-purpose rights period if transfer/commercialization is expected to take longer. Government purpose rights cannot be used for commercial purposes but can be used by other government agencies and in government contracts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limited rights for privately funded DOD technical data
rubrics_metrics.description: When technical data are developed exclusively at private expense and properly marked with the limited rights legend, the government is entitled to limited rights under DFARS 252.227-7013.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Costs charged to indirect cost pools are considered private support. Limited rights allow the government to 'use, modify, reproduce, release, perform, display, or disclose these limited rights data within the government.' The government cannot disclose such data outside the government or use them for manufacture except in limited situations (e.g., emergency repairs). Proper marking is required to preserve limited rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specifically negotiated rights must not be lesser than limited rights
rubrics_metrics.description: Alternative specifically negotiated license rights for the government may be negotiated for categories of DOD technical data, but the government cannot receive lesser rights through negotiation than it would under limited rights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DOD is prescriptive about marking and requires justification of restricted markings (DFARS 252.227-7013[g]). Contractors should be aware that DFARS sets specific legends and justification rules (252.227-7013(f) and (g)), which differ from FAR's approach to notices and placement.

rubrics_metrics.name: DFARS marking and justification requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: DFARS 252.227-7013(f) prescribes specific legends for government purpose rights, limited rights, and specifically negotiated rights; DFARS 252.227-7013(g) requires contractors to justify the validity of restricted markings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrast with FAR which prescribes content for limited rights notice but not placement. Contractors must mark DOD technical data correctly and be prepared to justify restricted markings; failure or incorrect marking can change the rights the government obtains.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of computer software and software documentation (DFARS)
rubrics_metrics.description: Computer software is defined broadly to include 'computer programs, source code, source code listings, object code listings, design details, algorithms, processes, flow charts, formulae and related material that would enable the software to be reproduced, recreated, or recompiled.' Computer software documentation means manuals and similar items regardless of storage medium.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Software does not include computer databases or documentation (the clause treats those separately). Understand these definitions when identifying restricted data in negotiations; delivery/rights consequences depend on category.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restricted rights specific to noncommercial computer software
rubrics_metrics.description: DFARS establishes a category of restricted rights specific to computer software that are narrower and more prescriptive than the limited rights applicable to DOD technical data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Noncommercial computer software is software that does not qualify as commercial under the clause. Universities typically deliver noncommercial software to DOD; the restricted-rights regime can limit later commercial licensing unless carefully negotiated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercial vs. noncommercial software distinction and consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Commercial computer software/documentation is that which has been or will be sold, leased, or licensed to the public. The DOD expects to use and license commercially available software on the same terms as the general public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commercial software should be acquired under the customary public license terms unless inconsistent with procurement law or user needs. Contractors are not required to furnish technical information not customarily provided to the public, except to document modifications made at government expense, and are not required to relinquish rights except by mutual agreement. Universities must be mindful of this distinction because labeling software as noncommercial in a DOD contract can limit future commercial licensing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Government rights determined by source license for commercial software
rubrics_metrics.description: DFARS [227.7203-3] provides that when software is commercial, the government has only the rights contained in the license under which the software was obtained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the government needs additional rights beyond the public license, it must negotiate with the contractor to transfer those rights. There is no prescribed DFARS clause for acquisition of commercial computer software—check the underlying license terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rights in commercially available items (DFARS 252.227-7015)
rubrics_metrics.description: When the government requires and receives delivery of commercially available items, components, or processes (i.e., sold/leased/licensed or offered to the public), the government obtains rights to use, modify, reproduce, release, perform, display, or disclose such data only within the government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The government does not obtain rights to manufacture additional quantities nor to disclose/use data outside the government except for emergency repairs or overhaul without prior written permission. Universities must ensure that both third-party license agreements and DOD contracts identify DOD's rights to commercially available contract data when such data are deliverables.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negotiation for enhanced rights in commercial data
rubrics_metrics.description: Contractors, subcontractors, or suppliers are not required to provide additional rights beyond those for commercially available data, but DOD may request negotiations for enhanced rights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the DOD desires enhanced rights, it may request prompt negotiation and, upon agreement, a license enumerating additional rights will be made part of the DOD research contract.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protection and marking of bid or proposal information (DFARS 252.227-7016)
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposal or bid submissions may include commercially important DOD technical data; if sensitive, steps must be taken to limit the government's rights by proper marking of proposal data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Submission without correct restrictive markings can be treated as a publication under U.S. and foreign patent laws and may result in the government obtaining unlimited rights (especially if contractor previously provided same data without restriction). The government may reproduce proposals for evaluation but may not disclose them to unauthorized evaluators; after award, the government can use proposal information within the government but not disclose outside without written permission. Proper marking is essential to protect patentability and trade secret status.

rubrics_metrics.name: DOE/DEAR distinctions and Alternate clauses
rubrics_metrics.description: DOE has historically claimed broader rights under the Atomic Energy Act; DEAR replaced DOE long/short forms with the general FAR rights clause but incorporates additional DEAR specifics (e.g., FAR 52.227-16 use and DEAR additions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DEAR distinguishes delivery of technical data from rights in technical data. FAR Additional Data Requirements (FAR 52.227-16) may be used for certain DOE contracts, giving the government rights to order data produced during performance or within three years of acceptance subject to withholding of limited rights data or restricted computer software. DOE may also substitute definitions and modifications (e.g., computer databases, enhanced software definitions) that expand its claimed rights compared with other agencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: DOE may require licensing of limited rights data/restricted software
rubrics_metrics.description: DEAR may include requirements for contractors to license to the government and third parties any limited rights data or restricted computer software at 'reasonable royalties' unless commercial equivalents are readily available (DEAR 952.227-14).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: University negotiators must watch for clauses that would require broader dissemination/licensing and should ensure that Alternate IV (which preserves university copyright) is used when appropriate for research and educational awards.

rubrics_metrics.name: DOE permission required for asserting copyright in first-produced software
rubrics_metrics.description: DEAR modifies FAR 52.227-14 by adding (d)(3) to require DOE permission for a contractor to claim copyright ownership in software first produced in contract performance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When permission is granted, DOE patent counsel must specify terms, conditions, and submission requirements to assure utilization, dissemination, and commercialization. DOE's (d)(3) may be used only in specified situations; universities should seek Alternate IV where appropriate and challenge departures.

rubrics_metrics.name: NASA NFS (d)(3) restriction and research exception
rubrics_metrics.description: NASA adds a (d)(3) restriction similar to DOE, requiring NASA permission to copyright/publish/release software first produced during contract performance, but the NFS states (d)(3) should not be used in contracts for basic or applied research with universities or colleges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NASA indicates FAR Alternate I for delivery of limited rights data may be appropriate for such contracts. Contractors seeking NASA permission must satisfy specified conditions and obtain concurrence of NASA Office of Aerospace Technology, Commercial Technology Division (Code RC).

rubrics_metrics.name: Grant/cooperative agreement default: grantee copyright ownership
rubrics_metrics.description: Under most federal grant/cooperative agreement regulations (and OMB Circular A-110 Section 36), grantees may copyright any work developed under an award; the federal awarding agency reserves a royalty-free, nonexclusive, irrevocable right to reproduce, publish, or otherwise use the work for federal purposes and to authorize others to do so.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Grants lack the detailed technical-data/deliverable definitions in procurement; research administrators should still watch for agency-specific provisions that incorporate FAR language or differ by statute. FDP terms largely follow A-110 Section 36.

rubrics_metrics.name: OMB Circular A-110 Section 36 — government and public access implications
rubrics_metrics.description: A-110 Section 36 gives recipients rights to copyright works developed under awards while giving the government a license to use data for federal purposes; Section 36(d) (Shelby Amendment) provides the public the right to request data used in developing agency regulations under FOIA.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies must request research data produced under awards and used by the government in developing regulations; recipients must provide such data within a reasonable time so they can be made available under FOIA. Administrators must understand when research data supporting regulations may be subject to public disclosure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'research data' and FOIA exclusions under A-110
rubrics_metrics.description: For purposes of A-110 Section 36(d), research data are 'recorded factual material commonly accepted in the scientific community as necessary to validate research findings,' and do not include preliminary analyses, drafts, plans for future research, peer reviews, communications with colleagues, physical objects, trade secrets, commercial information, materials held confidential until published, or personnel/medical records.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 'Published' is defined as peer-reviewed scientific/technical journal publication or when a federal agency publicly and officially cites the research findings in support of an agency action that has the force and effect of law. Understand these definitions when evaluating FOIA risk and when preparing data-sharing or publication strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: FDP terms and trend toward uniformity
rubrics_metrics.description: Federal Demonstration Partnership (FDP) general terms and conditions on rights in data essentially follow OMB Circular A-110 Section 36 and apply to member federal agencies' grants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For universities participating in FDP, FDP general terms apply to grants from member agencies. Although agencies may add specifics, there has been a trend toward greater uniformity among agencies on data rights under grants.

rubrics_metrics.name: NIH policy on data rights, sharing, and public access
rubrics_metrics.description: NIH GPS generally provides that grantees own rights in data from grant-supported projects, subject to NIH's royalty-free, nonexclusive, irrevocable license to reproduce, publish, or otherwise use the material for federal purposes and to authorize others to do so.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NIH encourages timely release and sharing of final research data (no later than acceptance for publication of main findings). Applications requesting $500,000+ direct costs in any single budget period must include a data-sharing plan or state why not possible. NIH public access policy requests authors submit final manuscripts to PubMed Central and encourages posting within 12 months. NIH also defines 'data' broadly and has policies on sharing unique research resources and model organisms; these guidelines are grant conditions and should be included in proposals.

rubrics_metrics.name: NSF policy: incentives to retain rights but expectations to share
rubrics_metrics.description: NSF normally allows grantees to retain principal legal rights to intellectual property developed under NSF grants to provide incentives for development and dissemination, while acquiring only rights needed to achieve its purposes. Grantees are expected to prepare and submit significant findings for publication and to share primary data, samples, and supporting materials within a reasonable time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NSF's standard copyright clause gives the federal government a non-exclusive, nontransferable, irrevocable, royalty-free license to exercise rights provided by copyright. In exceptional circumstances NSF may limit grantee control, but generally it preserves incentives for private dissemination and commercialization while encouraging sharing of data, software, and inventions created under the grant.
